ai.definition: Photonic computing refers to the use of light (photons) rather than electrical currents (electrons) to perform computations. This technology leverages optical components such as photonic transistors and waveguides to process information, potentially offering significant improvements in speed and energy efficiency over traditional electronic computing.
ai.howItWorks: Photonic processors utilize optical transistors that can switch light signals on and off, similar to how electronic transistors control electrical current. Waveguides are used to guide these light signals through the processor, enabling high-speed data transfer and processing without the heat generation associated with traditional electronics.
ai.problemSolved: Photonic computing addresses the limitations of conventional silicon-based electronics, particularly in terms of speed and energy efficiency. As electronic devices approach physical limits, photonic technologies can offer a pathway to overcome these constraints by reducing power consumption and enabling faster data transfer rates.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing photonic components requires precise fabrication techniques, including the creation of waveguides and optical transistors. These processes often involve complex lithography and deposition methods, which are typically carried out in cleanroom environments with high precision equipment.
ai.buildProcess: The build process involves several steps: designing the photonic circuitry, fabricating the components using techniques like epitaxial growth or chemical vapor deposition, assembling the components into a functional processor, and testing for performance and reliability.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the high precision required in fabrication, specialized equipment needed for cleanroom environments, and the complexity of integrating photonic elements with existing electronic systems. Research and development costs are also significant due to the novelty of the technology.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is promising but faces challenges in scaling and integration. While there are early prototypes and demonstrations, widespread adoption will require overcoming technical hurdles and establishing industry standards.
ai.regulation: Current regulatory frameworks for photonic computing are largely absent as the technology is still in its nascent stages. However, as it matures, regulations may be needed to address safety concerns related to optical radiation and compatibility with existing electronic systems.
ai.risks: Technical risks include the difficulty of integrating photonics with existing electronics, ensuring reliability over time, and managing heat dissipation at high speeds. Economic risks involve the high initial investment required for R&D and manufacturing infrastructure.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain due to the early stage of development and the need for significant investment in research and infrastructure. Once commercialized, photonic computing could offer substantial benefits but may face competition from other emerging technologies like quantum computing.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments will likely focus on improving integration with existing electronic systems, enhancing performance through new materials and designs, and reducing manufacturing costs to make the technology more accessible.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and high-temperature processes. Assembly requires moderate power for equipment operation but minimal additional energy beyond that.

glossary.def: An optical device used to switch light signals, analogous to electronic transistors.
A structure that guides electromagnetic waves (light) along its length, enabling the transmission of information over long distances without significant loss.
The process used in semiconductor manufacturing to pattern materials onto a surface using light or other methods.

subsystems.name: Light source
subsystems.role: supplies the coherent light that carries the signal; unlike electrons, photons must be generated, not just switched.
parts: III-V lasers bonded or grown on silicon

subsystems.name: Waveguides and routing
subsystems.role: guide light on-chip with very low loss.

subsystems.name: Modulators
subsystems.role: imprint electrical data onto the light.

subsystems.name: Linear compute fabric
subsystems.role: performs the arithmetic — mostly matrix multiplication, done by letting light beams interfere.
parts: meshes of phase shifters and couplers

subsystems.name: Nonlinearity and activation
subsystems.role: the hard part: light does not naturally interact with light, so nonlinear functions need help.

subsystems.name: Detection and readout
subsystems.role: converts the optical answer back into electrical signals.

subsystems.name: Control and thermal management
subsystems.role: keeps every phase shifter at the right operating point as temperature drifts.

buildSteps.title: Design the photonic circuit
buildSteps.detail: Each interferometer, waveguide and modulator is laid out with a foundry process design kit, then simulated for optical loss and phase errors.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the photonic chip
buildSteps.detail: Silicon-on-insulator wafers (typically a 220 nm silicon layer on buried oxide) are patterned with deep-ultraviolet lithography and etched to form waveguides a few hundred nanometres wide.

buildSteps.title: Add active regions
buildSteps.detail: Ion implantation forms the doped regions of modulators and phase shifters; germanium is grown in windows to make photodiodes, all in a CMOS-compatible foundry flow.

buildSteps.title: Attach the light source
buildSteps.detail: Because silicon does not emit light well, lasers are either bonded as III-V material in a separate process step or kept off-chip and coupled in through fibres.

buildSteps.title: Wire up control electronics
buildSteps.detail: Metal tracks and heaters are patterned, then the photonic die is flip-chip bonded or co-packaged with a conventional electronic chip for drive, memory and nonlinearity.

buildSteps.title: Package and fibre-attach
buildSteps.detail: Arrays of optical fibres are aligned and glued to the chip edge or grating couplers with sub-micron precision — often the most expensive step.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate
buildSteps.detail: Fabrication variation means no two phase shifters are identical; control software sweeps each one and stores correction values, then holds them steady against temperature drift.

buildSteps.title: Characterise and bin
buildSteps.detail: Insertion loss, bandwidth and bit-error rate are measured, and parts are sorted by performance grade.

prerequisites.why: CMOS-compatible foundries already make optical transceivers at volume, giving photonic computing a fabrication base.
silicon cannot lase efficiently, so light must come from bonded III-V material or off-chip sources, adding cost and packaging complexity.

prerequisites.tech: Optical memory and optical nonlinearity at low power
prerequisites.why: without a practical optical transistor or optical RAM, most schemes fall back on electronics for logic and storage.
the power and cost of converting between electrons and photons often dominate the system.
aligning fibres and coupling light on and off chip to tight tolerances is slow and costly at scale.

pathway.milestone: silicon-photonic transceivers and optical interconnects deployed in data centres
pathway.unlocks: proven high-volume photonic manufacturing and a reason to keep shrinking optical components.

pathway.milestone: co-packaged optics, where the optical link sits beside the processor instead of at the rack edge
pathway.unlocks: removes copper interconnect bandwidth and reach limits for large AI and cloud systems.

pathway.milestone: photonic accelerators performing matrix multiplication in real inference systems, with electronics handling activation and memory
pathway.unlocks: faster, lower-energy linear algebra where that is the bottleneck.

pathway.milestone: genuine optical logic and optical storage on chip
pathway.unlocks: general-purpose photonic computing, which depends on nonlinear materials and devices that do not yet exist.
